data.title: Trump says he’ll name an AI czar and create an ‘AI force’
data.description:
Trump says he will appoint a new AI adviser, without providing details

Reuters
Sat, September 19, 2026 at 6:33 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON, Sept 19 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump said in a social media post on Saturday that he plans to appoint a new artificial intelligence adviser, known as ‌an "AI czar," and create an "AI force," though he did not provide details about either ‌initiative or how they would be implemented.

Fears are growing in Washington among lawmakers about the risks posed by AI technology on ​humans and property. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said that "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI and argued that additional regulation is unnecessary.

"We will not in any way hinder or stifle ‌the Growth of this incredible Industry," ⁠Trump wrote on Truth Social, his social media platform. "Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows! However, we will also ⁠be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System."

Advertisement

If Trump follows through on the pledge, it would be his second AI czar. Venture ​capitalist David ​Sacks previously served in the role before stepping down ​in the spring and moving into ‌an external advisory position.

Sacks has echoed Trump's skepticism of new AI regulation. Speaking at a Politico event on Wednesday, he said AI developers should be responsible for ensuring the safety of their products and could be held liable if problems arise, adding that new federal rules are unnecessary.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump's post.

Trump's post comes ahead ‌of his scheduled meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on ​Thursday. Washington and Beijing are competing for leadership in ​artificial intelligence, which both governments view as ​vital to their economic and military strength. Trump and technology executives have argued ‌that excessive regulation would slow US AI development and ​undermine American companies' ability ​to compete with Chinese rivals, a claim that safety advocates often refute.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will meet with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on Sunday at JPMorgan Chase headquarters in ​New York to discuss AI ‌security, trade and other economic issues, a person familiar with the planning said on ​Saturday.

(Reporting by Susan Heavey, Waylon Cunningham, Matt Spetalnick, Courtney Rozen and Humeyra Pamuk; Editing ​by Sergio Non, Rod Nickel and Chizu Nomiyama )

data.title: MS NOW says its journalists were denied access to White House grounds
data.description:
After Trump ban, MS NOW says its journalists were denied access to the White House grounds

JOCELYN NOVECK
Updated Sat, September 19, 2026 at 12:33 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

NEW YORK (AP) — MS NOW said its journalists were denied access to the White House Saturday morning, a day after President Donald Trump said he would ban the network and two other news outlets from the complex. There was no immediate word about access for the other two — Politico and CNN.

The action escalated Trump's long-running efforts to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable, and is the latest test of First Amendment protections in the United States.

MS NOW said in a statement that it stands behind its journalists.

Advertisement

"The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars," the network said in a statement Saturday. "MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy."

Trump said Friday that he was barring the news channel, along with CNN and Politico, from the White House due to what he called unfavorable coverage and "fake news."

An MS NOW correspondent was turned away

It was unclear Saturday morning whether CNN journalists were also being blocked from the White House grounds. Network correspondents are usually present on the weekends when the president is in Washington or at nearby Camp David. Trump is at the presidential retreat in Maryland this weekend.

Politico journalists typically are not at the White House on Saturdays.

MS NOW White House correspondent Akayla Gardner was turned away, her entry badge confiscated, she said on air Saturday morning.

She noted she had walked through two gates successfully, but once she got to where her badge needed to be scanned, an officer told her it was disabled and asked her to hand it over. He said the decision "was above him," she reported.

An MS NOW producer was able to get in, but a photographer's badge was also disabled, Gardner said.

Trump calls these and other outlets 'fake news'

The president wrote on his social media site Friday that effective immediately, "I am banning" CNN, MS NOW and Politico "from the White House as a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" Minutes later, speaking at an event in the Oval Office, Trump was asked to explain his statement.

"Because they're fake news," he said. "You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news. When you look at CNN, it's just fake. That's why their ratings are no good. When you look at MS NOW … , it's fake news."

"And when you look at Politico ... the stories they wrote are fake. So there's a lot of news and there may be others to join them, and maybe they can get better," he said. "But our country has to have honest news."

In his second term, Trump and his administration have upped the ante and punished certain media outlets, both in the courtroom and through regulatory action. Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms.

The move follows the president's decision last year to bar Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events in retaliation for the news outlet's decision not to follow his lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters. The AP said that it would note when appropriate that Trump had ordered it renamed the "Gulf of America."

data.title: Denmark and Greenland push back on Trump's 'permanent control' claim
data.description:
Greenland, Denmark say US deal will not cede sovereignty

By Stine Jacobsen, Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen and Tom Little
Sat, September 19, 2026 at 11:46 AM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Special Report: How Trump's threats to seize Greenland have upended the island's push for independence

1 of 2
A drone view shows houses on the shore of Nuuk, Greenland, February 7, 2026. REUTERS/Stoyan Nenov

By Stine Jacobsen, Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen and Tom Little

COPENHAGEN, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, after President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington "permanent control" over the Arctic island's ‌security, leaving its precise scope unclear.

The United States, Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had entered into an agreement for ‌the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases on the island.

Advertisement

Key details of the agreement have not been made public, ​including the degree of US military presence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.

Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump's threats to seize control of Greenland.

"Next week could be a good week - for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States," Denmark's Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said ‌in a statement posted on Facebook on Saturday.

"A time ⁠of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe - while respecting the (Danish) Kingdom's red lines," he said.

Denmark and Greenland ⁠have repeatedly insisted that Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and accept that Greenland is not for sale.

TRUMP'S VISION FOR GREENLAND DEAL

Trump said on Truth Social late on Friday that under a deal, "the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend ​the ​security of Greenland, and the United States of America."

The deal "gives the United States permanent control ​over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," Trump said, ‌adding that no adversary would ever be permitted to have a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without Washington's express written approval.

Trump made the announcement after Reuters exclusively reported that the US and Denmark were closing in on a deal.

"This is probably not the end of President Trump's ambitions for Greenland and certainly not the end of US strategic interest in the territory and its resources," said Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen.

If Copenhagen cedes any formal power to Washington, it raises the question in Greenland of whether "this is the beginning of ‌replacing the colonial relationship with Denmark with a colonial relationship to the United States," he ​said.

Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said on Saturday that he was pleased with the proposed deal: "The ​agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our Kingdom and ​the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination," he said in a post on Facebook.

TENSIONS WITHIN NATO ALLIANCE

Trump's threats, which ‌peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis that strained relations ​within NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland ​into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.

A NATO spokesperson on Saturday said the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region."

Steffen Nielsen, a 49-year-old sales worker living in Copenhagen, told Reuters: "I think that the US is probably going to get ​what they could have had the whole time, if ‌they just asked nicely."

"I don't like it," Kaj Jorgensen, an 80-year-old pensioner, also living in Copenhagen, said of the news. "I don't wish ​the United States to be present anywhere in the Danish Kingdom. I really don't trust Donald Trump."

(Reporting by Stine Jacobsen and ​Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen, Additional reporting by Lili Bayer in Brussels; Editing by Ros Russell)

data.title: Aerial threat alert sounds in Saudi capital for 1st time in latest escalation with Houthis
data.description:
Saudi Arabia issues alerts across the country for aerial threat, and other Mideast developments

The Associated Press
Updated Sat, September 19, 2026 at 7:11 AM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Mideast Wars Yemen

1 of 3
A soldier from Yemen's Houthi rebels stands in front of a giant banner of the Kaaba, during a rally to protest Saudi Arabia's accusation that the Houthis targeted Islam's holiest site in Sanaa, Yemen, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (AP Photo/Osamah Abdulrahman) (AP Photo/Osamah Abdulrahman)

Saudi Arabia warned of a "hostile aerial threat" and issued a string of emergency alerts across the kingdom, including in its capital, late Friday and early Saturday.

Also Saturday, Iran's state TV reported that a man was executed after being convicted on charges of spying for Israel's intelligence agency Mossad.

Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Friday. Full coverage is available here.

Alerts sound across Saudi Arabia for aerial threat

Saudi Arabia warned of a "hostile aerial threat" after issuing a string of emergency alerts across the kingdom late Friday and early Saturday, and at least one explosion was heard in the capital, Riyadh.

Advertisement

The alert heard in Riyadh was first for the Saudi capital since the latest escalation with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

No casualties or damage were reported after the alerts were lifted. Saudi authorities didn't say what prompted the alerts or the cause of the audible explosions, but they previously reported intercepting incoming Houthi missiles and drones.

UN Security Council condemns Houthi missile attacks against Saudi Arabia and commercial vessels

The U.N.'s most powerful body said late Friday that the Houthis' military escalation, attacks and threats "risk further expanding the conflict, threatening maritime security and international trade" while undermining regional and international efforts to secure peace in Yemen.

It was warned that continued escalation would exacerbate the already dire humanitarian situation in the country.

The council's 15 members called for "practical cooperation" to prevent the Iran-backed Houthis from acquiring arms, military training, financing and other military-related assistance needed to carry out their attacks. They stressed that all countries must enforce the U.N. arms embargo against the rebel group.

Iran executes man accused of spying for Israel

Iran's state TV reported on Saturday that a man identified as Hossein Pedram was executed after being convicted on charges of spying for Israel's intelligence agency Mossad.

The report said Pedram passed on to Israel classified information on "sensitive military sites" in Iran's Isfahan province. It didn't say how he accessed the classified information.

Pedram was reportedly arrested after those sites, which included missile bases, were targeted in the 12-day air-war by the U.S. and Israel against Iran in June last year.

A recent surge of executions in Iran prompted an international outcry by human rights groups.

___

This piece will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

data.title: Oil prices are high but could be much worse. Trump has China's Xi to thank for that.
data.description:
Oil prices are high but could be much worse. Trump has China's Xi to thank for that

AAMER MADHANI
Updated Sat, September 19, 2026 at 4:08 AM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Trump Xi

1 of 4
FILE - President Donald Trump, left, and Chinese President Xi Jinping tour the Forbidden City, Nov. 8, 2017, in Beijing, China. (AP Photo/Andrew Harnik, File) (AP Photo/Andrew Harnik)

WASHINGTON (AP) — It could be much worse.

When President Donald Trump launched his war against Iran in late February, energy analysts issued dire warnings that oil prices could more than double during a protracted conflict and urged investors and motorists to buckle up for a bumpy ride.

The war grinds on and oil prices certainly remain volatile. But the most dire projections have not yet come to pass six months into a conflict that has no end in sight.

Advertisement

Chinese President Xi Jinping, who is making a much-anticipated state visit to Washington next week, could make a credible argument that the world has his country's energy strategy to thank for that.

It's unclear how much the two leaders will discuss Iran during the visit, which comes as Trump's Republican Party faces pressure from voters over high gasoline prices, and as China's buffer is being further tested as the conflict in the Middle East spreads. Trump, who has sought to keep a fragile trade truce with Beijing intact, has been careful in public comments about differences with Xi over the country's relationship with Iran.

"We've been free-riding off Beijing in a weird way," said Rosemary Kelanic, director of the Middle East program at Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank. "China's doing it because they understand that they're on the train that Trump is driving off a cliff. If oil prices go way up, that hurts the global economy. If it hurts the global economy, it hurts them."

China's stockpiles helped Xi weather the storm — so far

Beijing spent years and billions of dollars amassing the world's largest oil stockpile, building its strategic reserve to about 1.4 billion barrels by the end of last year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration's estimates. To protect China from foreign supply risks, Xi made energy self-reliance a part of the country's latest five-year plan.

Drawing from the massive stockpile allowed China, the world's second-biggest oil consumer and Iran's top buyer, to dramatically cut crude imports once the U.S. and Israel began their bombardment and Tehran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. The country was also helped by its shift toward electric vehicles in recent years and increasingly tapping into other energy alternatives.

China's oil import diet in turn helped ease global demand, softening the upward price effects for the United States, Europe and beyond.

"The Chinese deserve credit," said retired U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery, an analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank. "They did in 10 years what took us 25 years after the 1973 oil crisis to do: really build a kind of strategic petroleum reserve that could allow you to weather this."

But that resilience faces new challenges. Attacks by Iran-backed militias this month led Saudi Arabia to temporarily shut a vital pipeline that transports crude across the kingdom to ports on the Red Sea.

The Yemen-based Houthis have also seized two strategic islands in the southern Red Sea, bolstering the Iran-backed rebels' ability to disrupt a key maritime shipping route. Planned talks among Gulf nations focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which were supposed to take place earlier this week, have also been put on hold.

Before he meets Xi, Trump is set to meet Tuesday with leaders of the Gulf Cooperation Council in New York, on the sidelines of the annual United Nations General Assembly. The group includes Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait and Bahrain.

Oil industry experts say the moment remains tenuous

Analysts at Bank of America last week forecast oil at $83 a barrel for the second half of the year "in light of more persistent disruptions to Hormuz," but said they still expected shipping through the strait to gradually pick up.

But if violence escalates and keeps a chokehold on traffic, prices could reach $95 to $120 a barrel, while damage to major energy infrastructure could produce spikes of up to $150 a barrel, the analysts wrote.

Brent crude averaged about $69 per barrel last year and currently is hovering around $100. Brent crude briefly peaked in late April, touching $126.

How China has weathered the volatile oil market caused by Trump's war is ultimately seen by Beijing as "a vindication of Xi's last five-year plan and his focus on self-reliance," said Jonathan Czin, a former senior CIA analyst who is now at the Brookings Institution.

Deep differences between Trump and Xi on Iran persist

The war in Iran — and its impact on the global economy — is expected to be on the agenda for the Trump-Xi talks. But the prospects of the world's two biggest powers coming up with a breakthrough appear dim.

Over the course of the conflict, the Trump administration has faced resistance when urging Beijing to use its considerable economic leverage to press the Islamic Republic to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Chinese officials, who have expressed strong opposition to the U.S. war, also have bristled at more recent administration threats to ratchet up economic pressure on nations and entities still doing business with Iran.

To be certain, analysts say there's little altruism in how China came to sit on its massive stockpile of oil.

Experts believe Beijing was driven by contingency planning for potential military action to take over the self-ruled island of Taiwan, which China considers its own territory. Tapping the reserves now has been far from ideal for Beijing — but seeing global oil prices skyrocket was not ideal, either.

Trump treads carefully on differences with China over Iran

The leaders last met in Beijing just four months ago, and could meet twice more later this year.

After the talks in May, Trump claimed Xi agreed with him that a nuclear-armed Iran is a bad idea and that the Strait of Hormuz must be reopened. Chinese officials have neither affirmed nor denied Trump's telling of the private conversation.

The U.S. administration has also warned China not to aid Iran's military effort. But earlier this week, Trump downplayed a Wall Street Journal report that Chinese entities had supplied Tehran with satellite images of a Jordanian military base ahead of an Iran strike in July that killed three U.S. soldiers working there.

"You know, when they say that China spies on us, I say you're right, and we spy on them too," Trump told reporters.

Trump at the outset of the war called the conflict a "little excursion" that would last a matter of weeks.

He also has repeatedly predicted that oil prices will quickly plummet once the conflict ends. Less than three months into the conflict, he even declared "everybody was wrong" because the most dire projections for oil prices didn't come to pass.

The White House did not respond to queries on whether Trump credits China's actions with helping keep oil prices from hitting the worst-case levels.

But energy analysts credit Beijing's slashing imports as having the single greatest impact on moderating prices since the start of the war. China's crude imports averaged just 8.1 million barrels per day in the second quarter. That's almost 4 million barrels per day, or 32% lower than in the first three months of the year, according to U.S. data.

"It's remarkable how China managed the market," said Michael Lynch, president of Strategic Energy and Economic Research, a firm providing consulting services and analysis in the oil and gas industry. "They didn't panic and by turning to their inventories they kept the price down for everybody."

data.title: Is Trump's latest White House media ban legal? Recent history shows mixed signals.
data.description:
POLITICS
Donald Trump

Is Trump's latest White House media ban legal? It could get complicated

Aysha Bagchi Zac Anderson Joey Garrison BrieAnna J. Frank
USA TODAY
Updated Sept. 18, 2026, 8:59 p.m. ET

WASHINGTON – If recent history is the judge, President Donald Trump faces an uncertain legal landscape after his latest attempt to ban certain media outlets from covering him at the White House.

Trump announced in a Sept. 18 social media post that he is banning reporters from three major media outlets – CNN, MS NOW, and Politico – from the White House because he views their coverage as "FAKE NEWS."

Trump later said there wasn't a specific incident or story that prompted him to initiate the ban, which would not preclue the outlets from reporting on the president.

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," he said.

It's not the first time the Trump administration has taken such action against the press.

During his first term, the Trump White House in 2018 pulled the press credentials of CNN correspondent Jim Acosta, complaining that he refused to yield the microphone at a press conference. However, a federal judge appointed by Trump later forced the White House to restore the press pass, saying Acosta hadn't been given a proper chance to defend himself.

And in early 2025, the White House blocked the Associated Press from the Oval Office, The White House East Room, and the press pool that sometimes travels with the president. The White House was upset because the AP declined to change its style for describing the gulf bordering the U.S. and Mexico from the "Gulf of Mexico" to the "Gulf of America." Trump had ordered the name change on official maps.

In the AP's case, one federal trial judge appointed by Trump temporarily blocked the ban. But two appeals court judges - also appointed by Trump - on the three-judge panel reversed that decision in a 2-1 ruling. The case is still being litigated.

The past controversial decisions make for an uncertain legal landscape if the latest media outlets decide to take the White House to court for the most recent ban.

A spokesperson for CNN told USA TODAY in a statement that the ban Trump proposes would be an "illegal assault" on the press. The network said it plans to continue its coverage.

"CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting," the statement said. "We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government."

Politico, in a statement, said the publication "will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones" and "will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them."

Representatives of MS NOW declined to comment.

What has Trump said about the legality of banning reporters?

Trump dismissed concerns about violating the Constitution, telling reporters that the move is justified "because they’re fake news."

The president suggested he wanted to make a point, regardless of whether the ban withstands a court challenge.

"We'll see," Trump said when asked what makes him think his ban will be upheld in court. "I think it’s good to point it out, whether it survives or doesn’t . . . depends on the judge you get, to be honest with you. I don't think a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day."

“There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” Trump added. “Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine, but I don’t have to let them into my, into the people’s house.”

Trump had few details on what the ban means in practical terms ‒ whether it's the revocation of press badges, removal from the White House pool, or blocking reporters from the targeted outlets from entering the White House campus.

“A very simple ban," Trump said. "I don’t want them in my office, I don’t want them here. I would say the ban would go as far as you can.”

The president bristled when a reporter asked whether he's trying to intimidate the media from doing its job. "I dislike dishonest press, like you. I think you're terrible. I like to see honest press," the president said. 

Where does the AP's lawsuit stand?

The AP initially had success in its lawsuit challenging the Trump administration's ban. Washington, D.C. federal trial Judge Judge Trevor McFadden, who was appointed by Trump, ruled the ban probably violated the First Amendment's free speech protections and issued a temporary order blocking it.

"(U)nder the First Amendment, if the Government opens its doors to some journalists - be it to the Oval Office, the East Room, or elsewhere - it cannot then shut those doors to other journalists because of their viewpoints," McFadden wrote.

However, in a 2-1 decision governed by two other Trump appointees, Judges Neomi Rao and Gregory G. Katsas, an appeals court panel largely struck down McFadden's order. It said blocking the White House from restricting specific reporters' ability to join other reporters in the Oval Office or the press pool interferes with the president's authority.

"While the AP has alleged financial loss from being denied access to the Oval Office, that harm does not, inour view, justify an intrusion on presidential prerogatives during this litigation," Rao wrote, in an opinion joined by Katsas.

Judge Cornelia T.L. Pillard, an appointee of President Barack Obama, dissented, writing that her colleages' view "cannot be squared with . . . any sensible understanding of the role of a free press in our constitutional democracy."

Trump's latest targeted reporter ban appears to go further than the ban on the AP, barring reporters "from the White House," according to his social media post.

That may not hold muster even with the judges who largely ruled with the Trump administration before. Those judges did overturn an attempt by the White House to block the AP from accessing the White House's East Room, noting it is "a much larger space that can accommodate more members of the press." And those judges specifically noted the ban on the AP didn't block it from entering White House press facilities such as the main briefing room.

The AP's case is still under litigation.

What do experts say about the ban?

Clay Calvert, a nonresident senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, called the bans “thoroughly unsurprising,” particularly as Trump faces low approval ratings heading into the midterms. The institute is a Washington-based public policy think tank.

The news media is an “easy target” for Trump, Calvert said, and implementing the ban is likely to appeal to his political base that overwhelmingly distrusts mass media.  

Though it echoes Trump’s earlier ban on the Associated Press, Calvert described that as a “much more precise target” centered on a single decision – the news outlet refusing to adopt “Gulf of America” after Trump renamed the body of water widely known as the “Gulf of Mexico.” The ban was also limited to certain spaces, including Air Force One and the Oval Office. 

It's not immediately clear whether CNN, MSNOW and Politico would face similar restrictions or be barred from the White House entirely.

Barring journalists from the White House or other spaces where the government operates can make it “really difficult” to get information to report to the wider public, ACLU senior policy counsel Jenna Leventoff told USA TODAY. 

A federal judge blocked a press policy the Pentagon implemented in 2025 that said journalists who "solicit" information not approved for public release could lose access to the building. The Pentagon then imposed an interim press policy that required journalists to be escorted through the premises at all times, which was also struck down. 

But the potential to get involved in a costly and time-consuming legal fight with the Trump administration may make some news outlets “think twice” about their reporting, Leventoff said. 

“In that respect, it doesn’t matter if he wins in court or not, because he’s still chilling the media from saying things he dislikes,” she said. 

National Press Club President Mark Schoeff Jr. said in the organization’s news release on the matter that Trump “weakens one of the nation’s strongest checks on those who hold power” by blocking access to his administration.  

He said the latest ban would be an “unprecedented assault on press freedom” if implemented and underscored journalists’ role in informing the American public. 

“A government confident in its actions should never fear independent scrutiny,” he said.  

BrieAnna J. Frank's role covering First Amendment issues at USA TODAY is made possible by a collaboration among Freedom Forum, Journalism Funding Partners and the USA TODAY Network. Freedom Forum does not provide editorial input. Reach BrieAnna at bjfrank@usatoday.com and @brieannafrank on X and Bluesky.

data.title: Trump says U.S. has reached a deal to take 'permanent control' of Greenland's security
data.description:
1. News
  2. World
  3. Americas
  4. US politics

Trump says US has reached an agreement to take permanent control of Greenland’s security

Greenlanders have voiced their opposition to U.S. control, holding anti-Trump protests with signs that read, ‘Make Americans Go Away’

Rachel Dobkin in New York
Friday 18 September 2026 23:34 BST
  • Bookmark
  • Comments
    Go to comments

Bookmark popover

Removed from bookmarks

Your support helps us to tell the story

Support Now

From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging.

At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story.

The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it.

Your support makes all the difference.

President Donald Trump has announced an agreement with Greenland, in which the U.S. will take permanent control of the Arctic island’s security.

“I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Friday evening.

The president has eyed Greenland since before he returned to the White House in January 2025, arguing that the U.S. needed to control the semi-autonomous Danish territory for national security purposes.

Trump said that the agreement means the U.S. “will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America.”

It’s unclear what exactly is in the agreement Trump claims to have struck with Denmark and Greenland, but he did highlight one major point — U.S. adversaries such as Russia and China will need his approval to work with Greenland militarily and economically.

“From now on, no U.S. adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval,” Trump said.

The president had warned Russia and China would take Greenland if he didn’t step in.

“It's so strategic. Right now, Greenland is covered with Russian and Chinese ships all over the place,” Trump claimed during a press gaggle aboard Air Force One in January. “We need Greenland from the standpoint of national security — and Denmark is not going to be able to do it.”

Trump boasted about his role in the new agreement with Greenland that he said would be “cherished by the American People.”

“For over 100 years, Presidents have known the strategic importance of Greenland, but NONE of them were able to do anything about it. I am proud to be the President that permanently and conclusively addressed this very important situation,” he wrote on Truth Social.

“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many. We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction,” he added.

Since Trump began pushing to acquire Greenland, he has been met with opposition, not just from the people of the Arctic island and Denmark, but also from America’s European allies.

“Greenland belongs to its people. It is for Denmark and Greenland, and them only, to decide on matters concerning Denmark and Greenland,” a joint statement from seven European leaders read.

In the January 6 statement, leaders from France, Germany, the United Kingdom and other U.S. allies said, “We and many other Allies have increased our presence, activities and investments, to keep the Arctic safe and to deter adversaries.”

They said that since Denmark is a part of NATO, “security in the Arctic must therefore be achieved collectively...by upholding the principles of the UN Charter, including sovereignty, territorial integrity and the inviolability of borders.”

Days later, Trump threatened to impose a 10 percent tariff on imports from European allies, several of which were part of the earlier joint statement, “until such time as a Deal is reached for the Complete and Total purchase of Greenland.”

Trump quickly backed down from his tariff threats, claiming to have “formed the framework of a future deal with respect to Greenland” with NATO chief Mark Rutte.

Even with the new agreement between government officials, it is doubtful that Trump will sway those in Greenland opposed to American intervention.

The day Trump threatened tariffs against European nations if he did not strike a deal to acquire Greenland, protesters in Nuuk held Greenlandic flags and a banner that read “Make America Go Away” and “We Are Not Property!”

“I think he should mind his own business,” Greenlander Lars Vintner, a heating engineer, told the Associated Press in January.

“What’s he going to do with Greenland? He speaks of Russians and Chinese and everything in Greenlandic waters or in our country,” he said. “Every summer we go sailing and we go hunting and I never saw Russian or Chinese ships here in Greenland.”

A majority of Americans are also not sold on the idea of gaining control of Greenland.

Fifty-eight percent of Americans oppose a U.S. takeover of the Arctic island while 21 percent favor it and 20 percent are unsure, according to a Pew Research Center poll from January.

data.title: Trump's Kennedy Center overhaul has reshaped the venue and put its future in doubt
data.description:
Trump says the Kennedy Center could be 'ripped down' if he doesn't get 'recognition.' How we got here.

The iconic performing arts venue has been closed since Tuesday. A protest is planned for Friday night.

Andrew Romano
Updated Fri, September 18, 2026 at 9:07 PM UTC
11 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Trump was photographed this week on board Air Force One examining a large poster with the words "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED" printed above a rendering of a construction site, heightening concerns that his administration wants to raze Washington, D.C.'s iconic performing arts venue if his name is not added to its facade.

"I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition," the president told reporters before he boarded the plane Wednesday in North Carolina. "Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down." 

Trump's comments and the photographs that followed are the latest developments in a convoluted saga that started when he dismissed the center's trustees in February 2025 — just days after returning to office — and replaced them with loyalists who elected him chairman. 

Advertisement

Despite several legal setbacks, Trump's handpicked board has been pushing ever since to rename the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, which was built as a "living memorial" to the slain 35th president, after the White House's current occupant. 

The day before Trump was photographed with the "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED" poster, his appointees voted to close the center's main building for renovations. Does this mean Trump will bulldoze the Kennedy Center if he doesn't get the "recognition" he wants? Here's what we know — and what we don't.

Where things stand

The Kennedy Center is currently closed. Shortly after 4:30 p.m. on Tuesday, employees heard a sudden notice on the P.A. system: "The center is now closed to the public. Please exit the center by way of the Hall of States." In a statement, officials described the closure as a temporary, emergency action designed to protect people from deteriorating conditions inside the building after a five-foot-long section of ceiling plaster fell during a recent storm.

At the same time, the board has also been locked in a months-long court battle over its renaming and renovation efforts. Just hours before the closure, Federal Judge Casey Cooper again blocked the center from inscribing Trump's name on its facade — and the president himself responded on social media, saying that "the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place" unless an appeals court allows his name back on the building. 

"The closing will take place immediately, however, the Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board's approved name," Trump wrote. "If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place."

Last year, Trump demolished the East Wing of the White House after pledging that construction of his new $300 million, 90,000-square-foot ballroom wouldn't "interfere with the current building."

On Thursday, Cooper instructed the center to provide more than 30 days' notice before carrying out any significant changes to its renovation plan, "including but not limited to any 'demolition' of the center's main building."

On Friday, Kerry Kennedy — niece of President Kennedy and daughter of former U.S. Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy — posted on social media that a "Hands Around the Kennedy Center" protest would be taking place at 6:30 p.m. ET. 

"With the future still very much uncertain, now more than ever, the Center needs you to stand up for freedom of expression and against authoritarian overreach into arts and culture institutions," read the event's invitation. 

Trump takeover 

On Feb. 7, 2025, Trump announced on social media that he was taking over the Kennedy Center. "At my direction, we are going to make the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C., GREAT AGAIN," he wrote. "I have decided to immediately terminate multiple individuals from the Board of Trustees, including the Chairman, who do not share our Vision for a Golden Age in Arts and Culture." 

"We will soon announce a new Board, with an amazing Chairman, DONALD J. TRUMP!" he added. 

Within days, Trump had installed his former acting Director of National Intelligence Richard Grenell as interim executive director and replaced the bipartisan board with various allies, including Dana Blumberg (wife of billionaire Robert Kraft), Alison Lutnick (wife of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick), conservative country singer Lee Greenwood, White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and second lady Usha Vance.

At the time, Trump said he objected to previous Kennedy Center programming, citing "Drag Shows specifically targeting our youth." He vowed to oversee the performance schedule himself. 

"This marks the first time a president has removed his predecessor's board members at the Kennedy Center and installed himself as chair," the Washington Post reported. 

Previously, "political persuasion was never a factor we considered or discussed in artistic programming," Michael Kaiser, the Kennedy Center's president from 2001 to 2014, told the New York Times. "Our Board included 14 members of Congress who were evenly split between the two parties. This balance made it clear to everyone at the center that the only way for us to work was to ignore politics."

In response to Trump's takeover, musician Ben Folds and opera singer Renée Fleming stepped down as the center's artistic advisers; TV producer Shonda Rhimes — formerly treasurer of its board of trustees — left as well. Producers of the musical Hamilton and the play Eureka Day canceled entire planned performance runs. Other artists followed suit. 

"These events have caused a major negative reaction in my musical community to playing at the Kennedy Center," guitarist and composer Yasmin Williams wrote in an email to Grenell.

"I cut the DEI bullshit because we can't afford to pay people for fringe and niche programming that the public won't support," Grenell wrote back. Elsewhere, Grenell said that the center had "spent way too much on programming that doesn't bring in any revenue."

"We have completely reversed the decline of this cherished national institution," Trump claimed in August 2025. "We ended the woke political programming, and we're restoring the Kennedy Center as the premier venue for performing arts anywhere in the country, anywhere in the world."

Yet a Washington Post analysis conducted in October 2025 found that, after Trump's takeover, ticket sales for orchestra, theater and dance performances at the center plummeted to their lowest level since the COVID-19 pandemic.

A new name? 

In May 2025, the new Kennedy Center board revised its bylaws to exclude the 23 federal and local officials who automatically serve as ex officio members from voting. Going forward, only trustees appointed by Trump would be allowed to vote.

On Dec. 18, 2025 — shortly after Trump became the first president to host the annual Kennedy Center Honors — his appointees voted to rename the venue as The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts, or the Trump-Kennedy Center. Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the vote was unanimous, but Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, an ex officio board member, insisted that she "was muted on the call and not allowed to speak or voice [her] opposition to this move." 

The same day, a new logo featuring Trump's name appeared on the center's website; within 24 hours, workers had added Trump's name to the building's facade. "I was surprised by it, I was honored by it," the president told reporters when asked about the name change. "We saved the building." 

Justice Department lawyers later said the new signage had already been "prepared and/or purchased prior to the Board's vote the day before." 

In protest, more artists canceled planned performances, including Kristy Lee, Chuck Redd and Philip Glass. The Washington National Opera announced it would leave the center. 

"The Kennedy Center is a living memorial to a fallen president and named for President Kennedy by federal law," former Massachusetts Rep. Joe Kennedy III, RFK's grandson, wrote on social media. "It can no sooner be renamed than can someone rename the Lincoln Memorial, no matter what anyone says.

In late December, Beatty filed suit against the Kennedy Center trustees who voted to change the name, arguing that they had no legal power to do so.

A few months later, in May 2026, Cooper sided with Beatty and ordered the center to revert to its original name within 14 days. The center's founding statute "makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board's unilateral say-so," Cooper wrote in his opinion. "Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it."

By mid-June, Trump's name had been removed from the center's website and facade. But the board also tried to appeal Cooper's ruling, arguing that millions of dollars in donations would have to be returned if the center did not ultimately bear Trump's name, according to its new bylaws. 

These efforts failed, yet Trump's appointees seem undeterred. Last month, they voted to inscribe "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump" below the center's name on the building's facade — which led Cooper to again block the board from adding the president's name to the building. 

"Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing," Cooper wrote. "The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted."

Renovation or demolition… or something else?

In tandem with its renaming efforts, the board has also spent the last seven months pushing to shutter the center for renovations.

Trump started to muse about the project in late 2025. The following February, he announced the center would close on July 4, 2026, for a two-year renovation. "I have determined that The Trump Kennedy Center, if temporarily closed for Construction, Revitalization, and Complete Rebuilding, can be, without question, the finest Performing Arts Facility of its kind, anywhere in the World," he wrote on social media.

But in his May ruling, Cooper also issued a temporary order blocking the center from fully closing for two years. Instead, he said the center could "move ahead with renovations to the decades-old building and could later decide to close … after its board more fully considered the impact on its statutory requirement to maintain some programming at all times," according to CNN.

At the time, skeptics questioned whether major renovations were necessary, noting that Trump had previously said the center would remain "fully open during construction, renovation and beautification." 

"Trump's contradictory statements and the absence of an independent board or any notification to Congress make these claims of a building in need of repair unverifiable at best," the Atlantic wrote. "A more plausible reason for the closing is that under Trump, the Kennedy Center can't hold on to staff, artists or audiences." 

According to a Washington Post analysis published in August and based on confidential internal documents, "ticket sales had already dropped in the 10 months following Trump's takeover" — "but both ticket sales and donations plunged after the Trump-led board of trustees voted in December to rename the center after him and put his name on the front of the building." As of June, the center's own officials were projecting a $100 million revenue shortfall for fiscal year 2026, with a 70% decline in earned income, the Post reported. 

In response, Trump and his administration have argued that they inherited a "decrepit" structure in dire need of repairs — repairs that cannot proceed unless the president gets credit for them. 

"An order blocking the Board from appropriately recognizing President Trump will cause donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up and structural rehabilitation to stop," the Department of Justice wrote in an Aug. 29 filing, adding that without Trump's efforts, "the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down" — possibly to be replaced with "a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River."

Such a venue has "been proposed, by some, for many years," the filing said.

data.title: Trump says he's banning CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House
data.description:
Trump says he is banning CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House

WILL WEISSERT
Updated Fri, September 18, 2026 at 7:16 PM UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that he was banning CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House due to what he called unfavorable coverage, and threatened that more such media prohibitions could be coming — offering his administration's latest test of constitutional First Amendment protections guaranteeing the freedom of the press.

Trump has long bristled at news coverage he maintains casts him in a negative light, and has a history of filing lawsuits against news organizations, while lashing out at individual reporters in person or over social media.

The move follows the president's decision, in February 2025, to keep Associated Press journalists out of the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events too small for a full press corps, in retaliation for the news outlet's decision not to follow his lead in changing the Gulf of Mexico's name.

Advertisement

The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing. Since returning to office, however, Trump has pursued other legal action against a variety of different outlets, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC.

Trump seeking to block White House access for CNN is especially notably, however, as it could upend the traditional five-network television pool that travels with the president and tracks his every move — meant to provide independent coverage of his actions and interactions for the Americans who elected him and the world.

Trump wrote on his social media site that effective immediately, "I am banning" CNN, MSNOW and Politico "from the White House as a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

data.title: Democrats see a path to Congress as electoral worries spread into Trump country
data.description:
Why Democrats are starting to feel bullish about a midterm wave

Dan Merica and Theodoric Meyer, (c) 2026 , The Washington Post
Updated Fri, September 18, 2026 at 9:00 AM UTC
9 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Democrats' wary optimism about the midterms gave way to growing confidence this week.

The party has seen strong post-Labor Day polls in key battlegrounds - and even in traditionally red areas. Recent escalations in the war in Iran, including an attack on a major pipeline in Saudi Arabia, mean the rising gas prices bedeviling Republicans will not be going down anytime soon. Republicans have not been able to bring prices under control more generally. And President Donald Trump's unpopularity is at near-record levels.

Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.

Advertisement

Considering all this, Democrats now think conditions are right for the party to retake control of the House and possibly the Senate later this year.

"If the election were held today, we would win the majority," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (New York) said in an interview with The Washington Post.

Schumer said he felt "considerably more bullish" about Democrats' chances of retaking the Senate than he did a few months ago. He described the environment as uncannily similar to 2006, when discontent with the war in Iraq helped Democrats recapture the Senate and the House.

House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Massachusetts) said Democrats' recent momentum is driven by their focus on the economy, with voters believing that the party understands the financial pain they've felt in the years since Republicans swept into unified control.

"That is what is driving these polls," Clark told The Post on Thursday.

Still, Democratic fears remain.

Democrats need at least four more seats to take the Senate majority and would have to win at least two in states Trump carried by double-digit margins in 2024. Republicans are seeking to blunt any Democratic gains by flipping Democratic-held open seats in Michigan and New Hampshire, where polls show competitive races. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the Senate contest in New Hampshire from "Lean Democrat" to "Toss Up" this week.

Republicans focused on keeping control of the House argue that they have a more favorable map, partly because a GOP redistricting effort has limited the number of battleground districts, and partly because they believe that Democratic primary voters nominated weak candidates in a handful of key races.

Then there is the incoming flood of GOP money.

Republicans are set to spend nearly $140 million more on ads than Democrats are in the nine most competitive races in the final weeks of the campaign, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact. The disparity is especially yawning in the Senate contest in Texas, where Republicans have reserved $39.6 million in ads and Democrats have reserved just $5.1 million.

On the House side, the National Republican Congressional Committee plans to run coordinated ads in 39 districts, with more than $24 million in ads reserved.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has plans for coordinated ads in 14 districts.

"The Republican campaign engines are firing on all cylinders, and we are burying House Democrats in battleground districts across the country," said Mike Marinella, spokesperson for House Republicans' campaign arm. "Republicans have the historic fundraising advantage, a more favorable map, stronger candidates, and the firepower to defy history and grow our House majority."

Schumer acknowledged Republicans' financial advantage but said it would not stop Democrats from retaking the Senate.

"We don't need as much money as them given the political climate, given the terrain," he said. "All we need is enough to stay in the ballpark and be able to answer them."

Republicans have begun to openly acknowledge electoral concerns in recent weeks, particularly with polls showing that Democrats are far more eager to vote than Republicans are.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) told reporters Thursday that he was going to Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa to raise money for GOP Senate candidates.

"If you told me six months ago I was going to be having to spend my time in those three states, I wouldn't have believed you. Those ought to be fat guy layups for us," he said, though he predicted Republicans would hold those seats.

"The far left, they're angry," Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said this week on the "Pod Force One" podcast, describing this as a "challenging environment" for his party. "They hate President Trump with a burning passion. And they're going to crawl over broken glass to vote."

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) acknowledged Wednesday that Republicans are facing "headwinds" but said the Senate races that will decide control of the chamber remain competitive.

"It's not a great environment for us," Thune said. "But we've got really quality candidates in all the competitive races, and the polling that we're seeing in those races shows that these races are tight."

Republicans have been debating how to increase enthusiasm beyond spending more money. Some, largely those closely tied to the president and his political operation, argue that the path to victory is to re-create the electorate Trump built in 2024. Other Republicans - primarily those in battleground districts where private and public polls show that voters are deeply upset with the president - believe the way to win is to distance themselves from the administration and its policies, a difficult task following a decade of Trump remaking the party in his own image.

"I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump said during one of two speeches he gave at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas recently. "Just one more time."

Trump has made it difficult for many candidates, especially those in tight races, to embrace this tactic. In large part, that's because he has repeatedly dismissed the issue that voters say is their main stressor: prices. His trade war has raised prices on goods across the country. And gas prices, which have shot up because of the president's war against Iran, are nearing $4.50 per gallon on average.

However, speaking at a campaign rally Wednesday in North Carolina, a state he has won in three straight presidential elections, Trump said high fuel prices were "a very inexpensive price to pay for what we have done" in Iran.

A Republican operative working on House races, speaking on the condition of anonymity to be candid, responded to Trump's comments with an animated image of actor Bryan Cranston screaming, "F---!"

The president has promised to get out the vote for Republican candidates, including those in trouble deep in Trump country. Some have taken him up on his offer, but not every candidate wants him around, and administration officials' visits to red states have been seen as warning signs for Republicans.

Vice President JD Vance traveled to Kansas this week to stump for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who is in a tighter-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Trump and Vance won Kansas by 16 percentage points in 2024.

Vance is also set to campaign in Iowa on Friday. But the state's Republican Senate nominee, Rep. Ashley Hinson, will not appear next to the vice president. A Hinson spokesperson cited previously scheduled events, but the absence comes as the candidate seeks to tout her bipartisan record in a state Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024. Hinson is locked in a tight race against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek.

And in South Florida, an area Trump dominated in 2024, Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar openly broke with the president Thursday.

"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says directly to the camera in a new campaign ad. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

Democrats say they began to see a change during what was supposed to be Republicans' hallmark 2026 event: the party's unorthodox midterm convention. The gathering was billed as a way for the GOP to showcase its front-line candidates, but instead it featured Trump defending his record and pledging to give each American adult a $5,000 check if Republicans hold Congress this year, a proposal many Democrats saw as a sign of desperation.

"We're not measuring the drapes, but the ground has shifted," said Xochitl Hinojosa, a longtime Democratic operative and top spokesperson at the Democratic National Committee after the 2016 election.

Some Democratic operatives running campaigns said they had been waiting to see whether Republicans would coalesce around a clear affordability message during the Texas event. But when it became obvious that the event would be a Trump-centric celebration that offered no direct case for why Republicans deserved unified control for two more years, their confidence grew.

"Turns out breaking all your campaign promises and doing everything possible to make life more expensive for everyone is bad politics," said Viet Shelton, spokesperson for House Democrats' campaign arm. "Shocker."

The last time Democrats experienced a wave election was in 2018, when the party swept into control of the House two years after Trump's first presidential win.

Meredith Kelly, a Democratic operative who was the top spokesperson at House Democrats' campaign arm at the time, said that there are plenty of similarities between that year and this one - primarily around Trump's unpopularity - but that the biggest difference is how Republicans' worries are coming from voters who helped them win in 2024, such as rural voters and Black and Latino men.

"Their coalition's floor is falling out from underneath them," said Kelly.

The prospect of a wave election has Democratic candidates in districts once thought entirely unreachable for the party feeling like they may have a shot to do the unexpected in November.

Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy veteran running against GOP Rep. Lauren Boebert in a district that spans eastern Colorado, knows that her odds of winning have always been long. Trump won the district less than two years ago by 18 percentage points. But powered almost entirely by anger at Washington and voters' fears about their personal finances, Laubacher thinks she has an opportunity to take down her outspoken Republican opponent.

"People vote frequently about their pocketbooks and their wallets, but I think the situation is growing ever more fraught for people," said Laubacher. "Every aspect of their life has become more expensive, and they do not feel that the government is doing anything about any of it."

Jarrell Dillard contributed to this report.
